title: Henry Pleasants's review of her late-career singing
summary: Dance reads Henry Pleasants's praise of the album 'It's All Over Town' comparing her to Ethel Waters, Fanny Brice and Peggy Lee. Dance notes such writing was absent in the fifties.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Alberta had to say. But on the score of you know, you having something to offer and having made a comeback where you were able to show how much more you had to offer, I wanted to read to you; there's a man called Henry Pleasants and I don't know if you even know him. He's a very good writer and a very good critic and he said something about your comeback. He said, "that at an age where most singers are in decline, Helen is singing on this new album, and my memory of her at the International Jazz Festival last summer is better than ever. It's not just that the voice has more body, which it does, but that she gets deeper into a lyric than she used to. I have heard nothing on her earlier records that can compare with her heart-breaking account of the title track 'It's All Over Town', a pitious lament on a broken engagement. Here in a song characterization she is suddenly in a class with Ethel Waters, Fanny Brice, and Peggy Lee." And he goes on to say, "two exuberant uptempo oldies, 'Aint She Sweet' and 'Deed I Do', are pure joy, especially the former". Then he says, "a torch song, 'Good For Nothing Joe' is worth a second spin just to hear the way she belts out the line, 'She Beats The Hell Out Of Me'." And then he goes on and he quotes, " He May Be Your Man",

I thought that was very nice. But I mean, in those days, back in the fifties, before the end of the fifties, people weren't writing things like that.
But then it seems to me that it was when you made those Contemporary albums, that it first gave you an opportunity to show what you could do.
